articles.dek: Buy one share on NEPSE and three names show up: NEPSE, SEBON and CDSC. NEPSE is the market, SEBON is the regulator, CDSC keeps the record — here is who does what, and who to call when something goes wrong.

articles.title: NEPSE, SEBON, CDSC — three names, three jobs: who does what when you buy a share

articles.dek: On November 4 the NEPSE index rose 0.05% while 171 shares fell and only 98 rose. Breadth is the count that explains the gap — here is how to read it.
articles.image_alt: A stock-market heatmap board of green and red tiles, each tile one company's daily move
articles.title: The index rose and most shares fell — how to read market breadth on NEPSE

articles.dek: Global IME earned Rs 2.31 billion in the first quarter of FY2083/84 — the second-largest profit of any commercial bank — and its shares closed at Rs 266 on November 6. On that quarter’s annualised earnings and book value, the price sits below what its peers’ multiples would pay. On the audited full year it does not.
articles.image_alt: A street corner on Durbar Marg, Kathmandu, with commercial buildings
articles.title: GBIME at Rs 266: Nepal’s biggest bank, priced below both lenses — on the quarter’s earnings alone

articles.dek: Nabil Bank earned Rs 2.55 billion in the first quarter of FY2083/84. Five numbers — net profit, the change, EPS, book value and NPL — tell most of the story, and this is how to read them.
articles.image_alt: A hand using a calculator over printed financial charts
tags: How to read a quarterly report
articles.title: A Q1 report in five numbers — how to read what a listed company just filed

articles.dek: Exports rose 57% in the first quarter of FY2083/84 — but almost half of them were soybean oil refined from imported crude, and imports grew faster in rupees, so the trade deficit widened to Rs 532.49 billion. The record is real. It is also mostly re-export.
articles.image_alt: Stacked shipping containers at a container port at sunrise
articles.title: Nepal exported a record Rs 114 billion in Q1. The deficit still grew by a third.

articles.dek: Nabil Bank earned Rs 2.55 billion in a single quarter — more than any other commercial bank — and its shares closed at Rs 549 on November 6. On the latest quarterly figures, that price sits above what its peers’ multiples would pay for its earnings and for its book. The premium is real. The question is whether the quarter that justifies it can repeat.
articles.image_alt: Durbar Marg, Kathmandu, the avenue where Nabil Bank's head office stands
articles.title: NABIL at Rs 549: the biggest profit in Nepali banking, priced above both lenses

articles.dek: NEPSE is the secondary market. When you buy shares there, your money goes to the investor selling them — not to the company. The company is paid only once, when it issues new shares. The belief that buying on NEPSE funds the company is comforting, widely held, and wrong about the plumbing.
articles.image_alt: A trader watching market charts on multiple screens
articles.title: Rs 5,000 buys the shares — Rs 0 reaches the company: where your money actually goes on NEPSE

articles.dek: SEBON published the preliminary draft of the Intraday Securities Trading Regulation, 2083 on November 5 — same-day square-off, auto square-off, margin and exposure limits, feedback open until Mangsir 4, 2083. It is a draft, not a launch. The question is whether it raises liquidity or risk — and the honest answer is both, split by who trades it.
articles.image_alt: Securities Board of Nepal signboard, Khumaltar, Lalitpur
articles.title: 0.69% a round trip before you profit: SEBON’s intraday draft brings same-day trading to NEPSE

articles.dek: NIC ASIA Laghubitta earns Rs 7.01 a share, carries Rs 107.77 of book value, and trades at Rs 501 — 71.47 times earnings against a 28.53 times microfinance peer median, but 4.65 times book against a 4.80 times peer median. This analysis shows both lenses, every calculation, and the figures that did not agree.
articles.image_alt: NIC ASIA Laghubitta Bittiya Sanstha Ltd. logo
articles.title: NICLBSL at Rs 501: the market is paying for the book, not the earnings — 71.47× earnings against a 28.53× peer median

articles.dek: Balephi Hydropower earns Rs 7.72 a share in its first profitable year, carries a book value still below face value, and trades at 30.30 times earnings against a 45.21 times peer median. This analysis separates the cheapness the market is offering from the single year of profit it rests on, and shows every calculation.
articles.image_alt: A concrete hydropower dam in Nepal's hills
articles.title: BHL at Rs 233.90: below its hydro peers on both lenses — but the profit behind the price is only one year old

articles.dek: Nepal received Rs 2,363.13 billion in remittances in fiscal 2025/26 and just Rs 28.49 billion in foreign direct equity investment. The diaspora's money is already here; the channels that would turn it into investment are not. This article maps the one channel that works, the two now being built, and the five conditions that decide whether any of them scale.
articles.image_alt: Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu, with its terminal building and control tower
articles.title: Rs 2,363 billion came home last year. Almost none of it became investment — here is what has to change

articles.dek: NIC Asia Bank earned Rs 1.22 a share in FY2082/83 after losing money the year before, carries a 9.26% bad-loan ratio and negative distributable profit — yet at Rs 331 the market still pays 1.92 times book value, almost exactly the peer median. This analysis separates the price the market is paying from the earnings it is ignoring, and shows every calculation.
articles.image_alt: NIC Asia Bank's new corporate office in Kamaladi, Kathmandu
articles.title: NICA at Rs 331: priced like a normal bank on book value, priced like a crisis on earnings

articles.dek: The UN General Assembly has moved Nepal's LDC graduation from 24 November 2026 to 24 November 2029. The tariff hit is smaller than feared — India takes over 80% of exports duty-free anyway — but manufacturing is about 5% of GDP, production costs run about 30% above India's, and a 167-action transition strategy is still largely on paper. Three more years is not a reprieve; it is the last deadline Nepal can afford to waste.
articles.image_alt: The United Nations headquarters complex in New York, seen against a clear sky
articles.title: Three more years to graduate: the UN moves Nepal's LDC exit to 2029 — the last deadline it can afford to waste

articles.dek: Butwal Power Company has generated electricity in Nepal since 1966, pays a steady cash dividend, and holds just 19.40% of the 135 MW project now under construction in Manang. At Rs 712.30, the market is paying 72.4 times trailing earnings for that mix — this analysis separates what is operating, what is on hold, and what is still only a plan.
articles.image_alt: The Andhi Khola river above Waling, Syangja, flowing through green hills
articles.title: BPCL at Rs 712.30: the hydropower pioneer priced for a 601 MW cascade it only partly owns

articles.dek: In the first two months of FY2026/27, Nepali students sent Rs 29.55 billion abroad for education — 71.9% of all travel payments, and nearly twice the Rs 14.94 billion foreign visitors spent in Nepal. The annual record tells the same story at a larger scale.

articles.title: Rs 29.55 billion left Nepal for foreign classrooms in two months — nearly twice what tourists brought in
